messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Does completeness imply the nested-closed-set property?
If (F_n) satisfies the stated nesting and diameter condition and x_n \in F_n is chosen for each n, then (x_n) is Cauchy because, for any ε > 0, some N satisfies diam F_N < ε, and then d(x_m,x_n) < ε for all m,n ≥ N.
Completeness gives a limit x, and since the tail (x_n)_{n≥N} lies in the closed set F_N, we get x \in F_N for every N.
Thus x \in \bigcap F_n, proving the forward direction.
Does the converse hold?
For every Cauchy sequence (x_n), the sets F_n = \overline{\{x_k \mid k \ge n\}} are nonempty closed, satisfy F_{n+1} \subset F_n, and have diam F_n \rightarrow 0 because the diameters of those tails vanish.
Does the assumed property yield a limiting point?
The assumed property gives a point x \in \bigcap F_n, and for every k \ge n we have d(x_k,x) \le diam F_n.
Hence x_k \rightarrow x as k \rightarrow \infty, so M is complete.
